title: A segment tree with lazy range updates
prompt: Build a segment tree over ints that supports range update and range query. NewSegmentTree(nums) builds it, AddRange(l, r, delta) adds delta to every element in nums[l..r] inclusive, and SumRange(l, r) returns the sum of that inclusive range. Both operations must be O(log n): the tests run 400000 mixed operations over an array of half a million elements, so touching each element of a range is far too slow.
explanation: The whole trick is the lazy tag. A node's sum is always correct for the range it covers, but its children may be stale by the amount recorded in lazy[node]. An update that lands on a node fully inside [l, r] stops there: it adds delta*(hi-lo+1) to the sum and delta to the tag, which is O(1) instead of O(size). Anything that has to descend past a node first pushes that node's tag one level down, so the children are correct before they are read or written, and then clears it. Because a range splits into at most O(log n) fully covered nodes with O(log n) partial nodes on each side, both operations touch O(log n) nodes. The sum has to be recomputed from the children on the way back up, which is the line people forget: without it a partial update never reaches the root.
hints: Adding delta to a whole covered range changes that node's sum by delta times the range length, with no need to visit a single child.
Store the debt you owe your children on the node, and pay it out only when a later operation has to go through that node.
After recursing into both children on a partial overlap, recompute the node's sum from them, or the update never propagates upward.

title: Assignment cost by DP over subsets
prompt: cost is an n-by-n grid where cost[i][j] is what worker i charges for task j. Every worker takes exactly one task and every task goes to exactly one worker. Write minAssignmentCost(cost) returning the cheapest total. n goes up to 18, so trying every permutation is out, and picking each worker's cheapest remaining task is wrong.
explanation: The state is a subset of tasks already handed out, and the key observation is that the subset tells you how many workers have been served: exactly popcount(mask) of them. So the worker being assigned is not a second dimension, it is implied, and the table is one-dimensional over 2^n masks. dp[mask] is the cheapest way to give the first popcount(mask) workers precisely the tasks in mask; extend it by giving worker popcount(mask) any task not yet in the mask. That is O(2^n * n) time and O(2^n) space, which at n=18 is about five million steps against 18! = 6.4e15 permutations. Greedy fails because a worker's cheapest cell can be another worker's only cheap cell.
hints: The set of tasks already assigned is the only state you need; do not add a worker index to it.
How many workers have been assigned, given the mask? Count its set bits.
Iterate masks in increasing numeric order: every predecessor of a mask has fewer bits, so it is a smaller number and is already final.
